characteristics.name: Methods
characteristics.value:
Cluster-randomised controlled trial (cRCT)

Conducted from April 2007 to March 2008

characteristics.name: Participants
characteristics.value:
Clusters were families [n = 119 families: 300 children and parents (n = 52; children < 12 years)] of pregnant women who were initally followed up as part of the Pune Maternal Nutriton Study living in six rural villages near Pune city, India. 106 male and female children (9.0 ± 0.2 years) included in trial. Families were stratified according to the children’s baseline plasma concentration B12 concentrations with those below and above the median value equally distributed into 1 of 6 groups. 

Exclusion criteria: unwillingness to participate, pregnancy, anemia (hemoglobin per 100 ml), already taking supplements containing iron, folic acid and/or B12 for 10 or more days, or on treatment with drugs known to impair the absorption or utilization of folic acid or B12 (for example, phenytoin, antacids).

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
Intervention (n=197): families were assigned to 1 of 4 groups

  1. Vitamin B12 supplementation (B2F0; 2 µg/day)
  2. Vitamin B12 supplementation (B10F0; 10 µg/day)
  3. Vitamin B12 supplementation (2 µg/day) plus FA (200 µg/day) (B2F200)
  4. Vitamin B12 supplementation (10 µg/day) plus FA (200 µg/day) (B10F200)

Control (n = 103): Families were assigned to 1 of 2 groups.

  1. FA alone (B0F200; 200 µg /day)
  2. Placebo (B0F0)

Duration: 12 months

For the purpose of this review, the following groups were combined to create a single pair-wise comparison for meta-analysis: 

  • B2F0 and B10F0 versus B0F0
  • B2F200 and B10F200 versus B0F200

characteristics.name: Outcomes
characteristics.value: Haemogram (anaemia), blood glucose, lipid profile, serum creatinine, insulin levels, body composition (anthropometry including percent body fat), blood pressure. Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry, grip-strength, neuro-cognitive performance, arterial elasticity, food frequency questionnaire assessed among children at 12 months. Vitamin B12 deficiency, plasma vitamin B12, folate, and homocysteine at baseline and at 4 months, and 12 months.

characteristics.name: Notes
characteristics.value:
Setting (World Bank Region, WHO region, facility/setting type): South Asia, South-East Asia, rural villages

Compliance: monitored by counting the number of dispensed capsules and those returned at each monthly home visit (defined as taking ≥ 80% of capsules dispensed). 71% (n = 210) of participants returned < 20% of the dispensed capsules over 12 months. In addition, assessed by homocysteine concentrations > 10 µmol/l (in children), and vitamin B12 and folate concentrations < 150 pmol/l and < 7 nmol/l respectively. Compliance rates were comparable at 4 and 12 months.

Anaemia status at start of supplementation: B10F200: 22.2%; B2F200: 27.8%; B10F0: 11.8%; B2F0: 29.4%; B0F200: 27.8%; and B0F0: 22.2% (Hb <12 g/dL)

Vitamin B12 status at start of supplementation: B10F200: 38.9%; B2F200: 33.3%; B10F0: 17.6%; B2F0: 23.5%; B0F200: 16.7%; and B0F0: 22.2% (total vitamin B12 concentrations <148 pmol/L)

Form of vitamin B12: capsule

Vitamin B12 compound: cyanocobalamin

Funding source: Wellcome Trust, London, UK

Declarations of interest: no conflict of interest reported

Ethical approval: King Edward Memorial Hospital And Research Centre Ethics Committee on the 11th April 2006 (ref: KEMHRC/VSP/Dir Off/EC/065; Project No. 067)

We reached out to the corresponding author who provided us with unpublished data by cluster (age-stratified for children <12 years of age) and additional information for effective sample size calculation: 

"We have filled in the relevant data in the Excel sheets you gave us. If you need any additional information kindly let us know. Herewith attached is the document with the additional information requested. Let us know if you need further information. There were 106 families randomized based on the median plasma vitamin B12 concentration (188 pmol/l) of the children, to six groups (A to F). We are working on a paper where a secondary analysis of this trial is being done. Could you review the following data and let us know if this is enough? We noticed that the numbers in groups A and F are interchanged in the primary publication (flow chart: A, n = 50 and not 51; and B, n = 51 and not 50)."

Based on the information from trial authors, we calculated effective sample sizes for unpublished data for children < 12 years of age. To estimate the mean cluster size (M), we used the average total number of individuals randomized per family (children and parents) across all intervention groups. Sample sizes were adjusted accordingly, and sensitivity analyses were conducted using low and high intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC) values of 0.01 (Design effect = 1.49) and 0.05 (Design effect = 3.45), respectively.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

Randomised controlled trial

Trial conducted from April 2015 to February 2017

characteristics.name: Participants
characteristics.value:
600 male and female infants (6-11 months) attending immunisation clinics or residing in the Bhaktapur municipality and surrounding peri-urban communities near the capital Kathmandu in Nepal. Infants were allocated to 1 of 2 groups.

Inclusion criteria: "age 6 to 11 months, length for age z-score <−1, intent to reside in the municipality and surrounding areas for the next 12 months, and availability of informed consent from parents"

Exclusion criteria: "children taking (or planned to take) supplements that contained vitamin B12, had a severe systemic illness requiring hospitalization, if they were severely malnourished (weight for length z-score <−3), were severely anemic (hemoglobin concentration <7 g/dL), or had ongoing infections that required medical treatment. In cases of severe malnutrition, anemia, or infections, children received treatment and were screened again for eligibility after recovery"

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
Intervention (n = 300): vitamin B12 (2 µg/day) in a multivitamin (1 RDA of several vitamins and minerals) lipid-based paste 

Control (n = 300): multivitamin lipid-based paste alone (without vitamin B12)

Duration: 12 months

characteristics.name: Outcomes
characteristics.value: Neurodevelopment [BSID-III at 12 months, and WPPSI-IV and NEPSY-II at 24 months], attained growth (height, length-for-age, weight-for-age, and weight-for-length z-scores after 12 months, as well as growth velocity z-scores for the initial 6 months and the last 6 months of supplementation), markers of vitamin B12 status (total vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine concentrations), immediate adverse effects, and haemoglobin concentration at 12 months

characteristics.name: Notes
characteristics.value:
Setting (World Bank Region, WHO region, facility/setting type): South Asia, South-East Asia, immunization clinics or or residing in the Bhaktapur municipality and surrounding peri-urban communities

Compliance: monitored by asking mothers about intake of the paste during the past 7 days during weekly visits to the homes. Fieldworkers recorded the amount of paste given to the infants in detail (i.e. half, 1/3rd, 3/4th, or less), and counted the total number of empty paste sachets to verify the reported compliance. More than 94% of the prescribed doses were taken (94.3% in the vitamin B12 group; and 94.0% in the control group)

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Randomization was concealed, and the study double-masked as the participants were only linked to the intervention through the identity number printed on the supplement labels. The list that linked this identity number to the randomization code was kept with the producers of the supplements and the independent scientist who generated it. None of the investigators had access to this list until the data collection and cleaning for the primary outcomes were completed."

"Eligible children are allocated by block randomization (block sizes of 8) in a 1:1 ratio to one of the intervention groups. The vitamin B12 supplements and placebos have been produced specifically for this trial and are identical in taste and appearance. The supplements or placebos are offered in packages to the enrolled children according to a unique identification number provided by the company."

"The baseline features were evenly distributed between the intervention groups. The baseline status of vitamin B12 and its plasma biomarkers were also comparable between the intervention groups (S1 Table)."

Comment: There is indication that a third-party scientist was responsible for generation of random sequence suggesting the allocation sequence was concealed prior to assignment; in addition, vitamin B12 and placebo supplements were similar in appearance and taste. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. There is indication from Table 1 that baseline characteristics were comparable between groups; differences in nutritional status of infants (anaemia, wasting, underweight) may be compatible with chance findings.

characteristics.name: Participants

1000 male and female children (6-30 months) residing in urban neighborhoods of Tigri, and Dakshinpuri in New Delhi, India. Children were allocated to 1 of 4 groups.

Intervention (n = 500): children were allocated to 1 of 2 groups.

  2. Placebo

Number of episodes of acute lower respiratory infections, and diarrhea, morbidity (proportion of children with at least one reported illness) at baseline and two times/week for 6 months. risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid-based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp)."

"The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. Author report and visual inspection of Table 1 suggests no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Any observable differences are compatible with chance findings.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "Included children were randomized to 3 groups to receive one bar per day, fortified mg with (a) 2 B12 or (b) multiple micronutrients mg (MMN), including 1.82 B12 (United Nations 12 Children’s Emergency Fund guidelines (Supplementary Table 1), or (c) no added micronutrients (placebo). All bars were similar in appearance."

"Randomization was computer generated, and stratification was based on baseline B12 and hemoglobin concentrations (below and above median) to ensure comparable distribution."

"We approached 180 school children and their parents to participate in the trial, of whom 178 (99%) agreed. Fourteen children were excluded: 13 with B12 <100 pmol/L and 1 with anemia; they were prescribed appropriate treatment (Figure 1A). The 164 randomized children (57% girls) were 11.3 (10.9-12.0) years old, 139.4 (134.5-144.5) cm tall and with a weight of 28.8 (25.2-33.4) kg; there was no significant difference between groups. Plasma B12, folate, and homocysteine concentrations were comparable (Table 1)."

Comment: The method of allocation concealment were not reported; however, nutrient composition of nutrient bars were probably concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a sound method of random number generation. Authors report no differences in baseline characteristics between intervention groups.
